transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Doctor, I’m here because this has been going on for months now, and I don’t think it’s something I can just ignore anymore. It’s the property manager, and not just him—certain people in the building too. There’s a pattern. It’s not one isolated thing.

It started with the mail, or at least that’s when I really began noticing it. Things being misdelivered, things that should have come to me turning up strangely, or neighbors making little comments that sounded casual but were clearly connected. Then there are noises in the walls, timed in a way that’s too precise—right when I’m doing something, or when I’m about to settle down. And then someone will say something in the hallway the next day, just a small remark, but it lines up with what happened.

They keep giving explanations—paperwork, building notices, excuses about maintenance or mail mix-ups—but none of that changes the overall pattern. I was a management analyst for years; I know how to look at repeated events and see when something isn’t random. And what I see is pressure. They’re trying to push me out of my apartment without coming right out and saying it.
Aside from the noises in the walls that you believe are timed deliberately, have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people around you say they don't hear?

Voices? No, I wouldn’t put it that way. I’m not sitting in my apartment hearing some voice talking to me, if that’s what you mean.

The sounds I’m talking about are actual sounds in the building—pipes, knocking, scraping, things in the wall or ceiling, that sort of thing. And yes, if I ask someone else about it, they’ll usually shrug or say they didn’t notice, but that doesn’t mean it didn’t happen. People don’t always pay attention. Or they don’t want to get involved.

So, no, not voices exactly. It’s more that the timing of the noises is what stands out to me. That’s the part people keep trying to wave away.

Has this feeling that people are targeting you always been part of how you generally view others and interact with the world, or did you notice a clear change—like before a certain point you didn't feel this way, and then it started?

No, I wouldn’t say it’s always been how I viewed people. I mean, I’ve never been naïve—when you work as a management analyst, you learn to notice patterns and incentives, and you don’t just accept everything at face value. But this particular feeling, that people in the building are targeting me, that wasn’t just my general outlook on life.

It really started after I moved into this apartment. Not immediately the first day, but shortly after. And it’s been going on about 11 months now, give or take. Before that, I had normal disagreements with people like anyone else, but I wasn’t walking around thinking neighbors or management were coordinating against me. This is tied to what’s been happening since I came here.
Do you have any medical conditions—like thyroid problems, seizures, or head injuries—or have you been using any drugs, alcohol, or new medications around the time these beliefs started?

I don’t know that I can give you a neat medical explanation for it. I mean, I understand why you’re asking—thyroid, seizures, head injuries, medications, that sort of thing—but nothing like that jumps out to me as the cause.

I haven’t been thinking of this as something that started because of a pill or because I drank something or hit my head. It started because of what was happening in the building. That’s the sequence as I experienced it. I moved there, things began to happen, and then the pattern became clearer over time.

As far as drugs or alcohol, no, there wasn’t some big change around then that I can point to. Same with new medications—I can’t think of anything that suddenly changed and then all this began. If there’s something specific you want me to check or remember, I can try, but from my point of view this isn’t coming from my body playing tricks on me.

Since these beliefs about your neighbors and the building started, have you noticed any change in your ability to manage daily responsibilities—like your job, self-care, or relationships with people outside the building?

Yes, I suppose there has been a change, though I don’t like framing it as if I’ve simply “stopped functioning.” I still take care of myself, I’m not just lying in bed or anything like that. But my time has definitely been… diverted, I guess is the word.

Before all this, I had a pretty normal rhythm. I’d do my consulting work, keep up with professional contacts, and I used to paint more regularly—just as a routine, something that kept me grounded. Since this started, I’ve pulled back from several consulting jobs because I can’t properly focus on them when I’m constantly having to follow up on what’s going on here. It’s not that I suddenly forgot how to work. It’s more that a huge portion of my week gets swallowed by documenting things, talking to neighbors, contacting the office, trying to get building staff to acknowledge patterns, going back over emails, that sort of thing.

And relationships outside the building… I still have them, but I probably talk less about ordinary things than I used to. My attention keeps getting dragged back to this situation. So yes, my normal work and painting routine have been pushed aside more than I’d like. I wouldn’t say I’m incapable, but I’m definitely not living the way I was before.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a single, well-organized, non-bizarre persecutory delusional system (neighbors/property manager coordinating to force her out) lasting approximately 11 months. She denies auditory or other hallucinations, and there is no history of prominent mood episodes, disorganized speech, or negative symptoms typical of schizophrenia. Functioning is impaired specifically in domains related to the delusional preoccupation (reduced consulting work, less painting, hypervigilance to building events), but self-care and baseline social relationships remain largely intact, consistent with the relatively circumscribed impairment seen in delusional disorder rather than the broader deterioration of schizophrenia. No general medical condition, head injury, seizure disorder, or substance use was identified as a cause, and the belief system represents a change from her prior baseline personality/worldview rather than a lifelong pattern of suspiciousness (excluding paranoid personality disorder). These features are most consistent with Delusional Disorder, persecutory type (F22).
